newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs futures end up but off highs, buoyed by cash.
newsitem.headline: JGBs futures end up but off highs, buoyed by cash.

text.p: The benchmark September 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) futures contract ended Thursday trade firmer but off earlier highs, buoyed by solid buying of cash bonds and continuing positive sentiment, traders said.

Gains were dented by the end of morning trade on sales due to rumours, later denied, that an influential Finance Ministry official might make comments hinting at a rate rise. But short-covering due to futures' inability to fall even under these circumstances helped erase losses in the afternoon.
Good buying of cash bonds, including 20-year bonds, also gave futures buoyancy. But the topside was heavy near 126.60.

"We've seen pretty good buying of the super-long end for the second day in a row -- mainly by life insurers, although other institutional investors are also taking part -- and this is giving the whole market a firm tone," one trust bank trader said.

Key September finished at 126.45, up 0.24 from Wednesday's Tokyo close. It briefly hit 126.54 in morning trade but then recoiled in the face of sales sparked by rumours, mainly from overseas, that Vice Finance Minister Eisuke Sakakibara might indicate a rate rise. But ministry officials said he was on holiday and was not expected to make any official speeches.

"Actually, I think it was merely a good level at which to take profits, and that the Sakakibara talk was tacked on later to provide an excuse," one trader said, noting futures did not give up all their gains even under these conditions.
Even though a renewed topside try in afternoon was blocked, traders said sentiment remained firm overall and that a challenge of 127 might not be all that far away.

A fairly large volume of outstanding call options was said to be lined up at 127.00 and then 128.00, traders said. If September rose towards these levels, buy-back demand would emerge from sellers of the call options, fuelling more rises.
Yield on the benchmark 182nd 10-year cash bond edged down towards its April record low of 2.075 percent but stalled at 2.100 percent before rising slightly again.
By 0623 GMT it stood at 2.115 percent against 2.125 percent at Wednesday's close.

Although some traders said the key bond yield could well attempt a new record low soon, others felt this is unlikely over the short term. "To see yields like that in cash bonds, we'd have to have the key futures contract rise at least to 127, which seems difficult right now without some sort of fresh factor," the trust bank trader said.
